title: Klonopin and Alcohol: Why Clonazepam Lingers Into the Next Day
excerpt: Can you drink on Klonopin? How clonazepam and alcohol stack up in the brain, why its 30-40 hour half-life means it is still active tomorrow, and the warning signs that need 911.
metaDescription: Can you drink on Klonopin? How clonazepam and alcohol interact, why its long half-life carries into the next day, and the overdose signs that need 911.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** Klonopin (clonazepam) and alcohol should not be mixed. Both slow down your brain through the same calming chemical system, and together they add up to more sedation, more memory loss, and slower breathing than either one causes alone. The thing that makes Klonopin different from many other anxiety medicines is how long it lasts. Clonazepam has a half-life of roughly 30 to 40 hours, which means a dose you took yesterday morning is still working in your body tonight. "I'll just skip my pill before I go out" doesn't give you the clean break it sounds like.

**The quick rules:** Don't drink on the same day as a Klonopin dose, and don't assume a missed or skipped dose has cleared your system. Never take Klonopin to calm hangover anxiety or to get to sleep after drinking. Never stop Klonopin suddenly so you can drink, because stopping abruptly can cause withdrawal, including seizures. If you're not sure how alcohol fits with your prescription, ask the doctor who prescribed it or your pharmacist. They know your dose and your history.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains how clonazepam and alcohol interact in general terms. It is not a substitute for your prescriber or pharmacist. **Talk to your doctor before drinking at all if** you take Klonopin or generic clonazepam, take it for seizures, also take an opioid, sleep medicine, gabapentin, or another sedating drug, are an older adult, or have liver or lung disease. **Call 911 right away if** someone who took Klonopin and drank can't be woken, is breathing very slowly or with long pauses, has blue or gray lips, or is having a seizure.

## How Klonopin and Alcohol Interact: The Mechanism in Plain Words

Your brain has a built-in brake pedal called **GABA**, the main chemical that tells nerve cells to quiet down. Much of that braking happens at a docking site on nerve cells called the **GABA-A receptor**. When GABA locks onto it, a small channel opens and the cell becomes harder to fire. That's what calm, drowsy, and relaxed feel like at the chemical level.

**Clonazepam** is a benzodiazepine. It attaches to its own spot on the GABA-A receptor and makes GABA work harder, so each time GABA arrives the channel opens more often. More braking means less anxiety, fewer panic attacks, and, in people with certain seizure disorders, fewer seizures. That's exactly why it's prescribed.

**Alcohol** pushes on the same brake. It also boosts GABA-A activity, and at the same time it dampens **glutamate**, the brain's main accelerator. So alcohol presses the brake and lifts off the gas at once.

Put the two together and you're pressing the same pedal from two directions. The effects don't just sit side by side. They stack, and in some people they stack more than you'd predict from adding the two separately. The parts of the brain that this affects include:

- **The thinking and judgment areas**, which is why people feel far more impaired than their drink count suggests
- **The memory-forming areas**, which is why blackouts are common with this combination
- **The brainstem, which runs your breathing.** This is the dangerous one. Benzodiazepines on their own rarely stop someone's breathing at normal doses. Alcohol on top changes that, because both drugs slow the breathing drive, and the reflexes that would normally wake you when your oxygen drops are blunted too.

There's a smaller second layer. Clonazepam is broken down in the liver, mainly by an enzyme called **CYP3A4**. Heavy drinking, liver disease, and some other medicines can change how fast that happens. But the main danger isn't about the liver. It's the two drugs piling onto the same brake system in the brain.

## What the Label and Official Guidance Say

You don't have to take anyone's word for this. The official prescribing information is clear.

- **The label tells patients to avoid alcohol.** Klonopin's US prescribing information warns that it can add to the effects of alcohol and other central nervous system depressants, and that patients should avoid alcohol while taking it.
- **There is an FDA boxed warning on all benzodiazepines.** In 2016 the FDA added its strongest warning, a boxed warning, about combining benzodiazepines with opioids because of the risk of profound sedation, slowed breathing, coma, and death. In 2020 the FDA expanded the boxed warning on the whole class to cover abuse, misuse, addiction, physical dependence, and withdrawal reactions. Alcohol isn't the subject of that box, but the reasoning is the same: two drugs that slow breathing are more dangerous together.
- **Driving and machinery.** The label warns against driving or operating machinery until you know how clonazepam affects you. Alcohol makes that impairment worse and less predictable.

Emergency department and overdose data collected by US public health agencies have repeatedly found alcohol involved in a large share of benzodiazepine-related emergencies and deaths. The pattern is consistent: serious harm from benzodiazepines usually happens when they're combined with something else that slows breathing, most often opioids or alcohol.

## Klonopin's Long Half-Life: Why It's Still in You the Next Day

This is the part most people underestimate, and it's the main thing that separates Klonopin from Xanax.

A drug's **half-life** is the time it takes your body to clear half of it. Clonazepam's half-life is typically quoted as **about 30 to 40 hours** in the prescribing information, and it can be longer in some people. Compare that with immediate-release alprazolam (Xanax), which averages around 11 hours.

What that means in practice:

- **Blood levels peak within about 1 to 4 hours** after you swallow a tablet, which is when sedation is usually strongest.
- **A day later, a large share of that dose is still in your blood.** You may not feel "on" it anymore, but it's still working on your GABA system.
- **If you take it every day, it builds up.** With a half-life this long, it takes the better part of a week of regular dosing to reach a steady level. People on a daily schedule effectively always have clonazepam in their system.
- **Older adults, people with liver disease, and people on certain other medicines** can clear it more slowly still.

So the common plan of "I'll skip tonight's dose and have a few drinks" doesn't create a clean gap. If you take clonazepam daily, you'll still be carrying most of it when you drink. And skipping doses brings its own problems, covered below.

## How Long After Taking Klonopin Can You Drink?

There is no official waiting period that's safe for everyone, and anyone giving you an exact number of hours is guessing. What can be said with confidence:

- **If you take Klonopin daily, there's no "between doses" window.** The drug never fully clears while you're taking it regularly. This is the situation where the label's "avoid alcohol" advice applies most directly.
- **If you took a single dose "as needed,"** a meaningful amount will still be in your system for well over a day. Because the half-life is so long, it takes several days for a single dose to clear almost completely.
- **Feeling normal isn't a reliable signal.** Your sense of being "back to normal" fades long before the drug's effect on your breathing and reaction time does.

The right person to ask is your prescriber or pharmacist. They know your dose, your schedule, your other medicines, and your health, and they can tell you what's sensible for your specific situation. If you know a wedding, holiday, or trip is coming up, ask ahead of time rather than improvising on the night.

## Is One Drink Okay on Klonopin?

This is one of the most searched versions of the question, and the honest answer is that **there's no amount of alcohol known to be safe with clonazepam.** The label doesn't give a "safe" number of drinks, and neither does any major medical body.

So the answer to "is one drink okay?" is no. Don't combine them. Because clonazepam lingers for more than a day, that means no alcohol on any day you're taking it, not just the hours right after a pill. If you're struggling to go without alcohol while you're on clonazepam, tell your prescriber. That's important information for them, not something to manage on your own.

If someone has already mixed the two and is very drowsy, confused, hard to wake, or breathing slowly, treat it as an emergency and call 911. The warning signs are listed below.

## What Happens If You Mix Klonopin and Alcohol?

The effects depend on how much of each, the timing, your body size, whether you've eaten, how used to clonazepam you are, and what else is in your system. That unpredictability is a big part of the danger. In rough order from milder to severe:

1. **Strong drowsiness and feeling "much drunker" than expected.** People often describe feeling hit hard by a small number of drinks.
2. **Poor coordination, slurred speech, and slowed reactions.** Falls and injuries are common, especially in older adults.
3. **Memory gaps and blackouts.** Both drugs interfere with forming new memories, and together they make blackouts more likely. People may seem awake and talk normally but remember nothing later. Our guide to [blackouts from drinking](/never-hungover/blackout-drunk) explains what's happening in the brain.
4. **Disinhibition and poor judgment.** Some people become uncharacteristically impulsive or agitated rather than sleepy.
5. **Vomiting while sedated.** Someone who is heavily sedated may not wake up or protect their airway if they vomit.
6. **Slow, shallow breathing, coma, and death.** This is the outcome the warnings exist to prevent.

### The "sleeping it off" trap

The most dangerous moment is often after someone goes to bed. A person who seems to be sleeping can be breathing more and more slowly. If you're with someone who took Klonopin and has been drinking heavily, don't leave them alone to sleep it off if they're very hard to rouse. Lay them on their side and check on them, and call 911 if their breathing is slow or irregular.

## Klonopin for Hangover Anxiety or Sleep After Drinking

This is a real and understandable temptation. Alcohol often causes a rebound the next morning, sometimes called hangxiety: as alcohol wears off, the brain's brake system is temporarily underpowered and its accelerator is overactive. The result is a racing mind, dread, and poor sleep. If you already have a Klonopin prescription for panic or anxiety, reaching for one seems logical.

It's still a bad idea, for three reasons:

- **Alcohol may still be in your blood.** After a heavy night, you can still have alcohol on board well into the next morning, so you'd be combining the two after all.
- **It treats the rebound with more of the same.** Using a sedative to calm the rebound from another sedative can turn into a pattern where each makes the other feel necessary.
- **In regular heavy drinkers, morning shakiness and anxiety can be early alcohol withdrawal.** That needs a doctor's assessment, not self-medication.

The same goes for taking Klonopin to get to sleep after drinking. Alcohol already disrupts sleep, especially the second half of the night, and adding clonazepam on top of alcohol at bedtime is exactly the combination that leads to slowed breathing during sleep. Our guide to [why you can't sleep after drinking](/never-hungover/cant-sleep-after-drinking) covers safer ways to handle a wired, sleepless night, and the [hangxiety guide](/never-hungover/hangxiety-complete-guide-2026-supplements-research) explains why the morning-after anxiety happens and what helps.

If hangover anxiety is a regular problem, that's useful information to bring to your prescriber. It's also a sign that the amount you're drinking is working against the condition your medication is treating.

## Clonazepam and Alcohol: Special Situations

### If you take Klonopin for seizures

Clonazepam is approved for certain seizure disorders, and this group has extra reasons to be careful. Heavy drinking, the sleep loss that comes with a night out, and alcohol wearing off can all make seizures more likely. Missing doses of clonazepam can do the same. Combining those factors can undo the seizure control your medication provides. If you take clonazepam for epilepsy, talk to your neurologist specifically about alcohol.

### If you take Klonopin for panic disorder or anxiety

Alcohol can feel like it calms anxiety in the moment, but it tends to make anxiety worse over the following day and, with regular use, over time. Drinking can work against the very condition clonazepam is treating. Our guide to [alcohol and anxiety](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-anxiety-breaking-the-cycle-naturally-2025) explains that cycle.

### If you're an older adult

Older adults are more sensitive to benzodiazepines, clear them more slowly, and are at higher risk of falls, confusion, and fractures. The American Geriatrics Society's Beers Criteria, a widely used list of medicines to use with caution in older people, lists benzodiazepines among drugs to generally avoid. Adding alcohol raises those risks further.

### Mood and depression

Like other seizure medicines, clonazepam's label carries a warning about watching for new or worsening depression or suicidal thoughts. Alcohol is also a depressant that can worsen low mood. If you notice your mood dropping, tell your prescriber. If you're having thoughts of harming yourself, call or text **988** (the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline in the US) or go to an emergency room.

## Klonopin, Alcohol, and Other Sedating Medicines

The risk climbs with every additional substance that slows the brain. Adding any of these to Klonopin and alcohol makes things more dangerous:

- **Opioid painkillers** such as oxycodone, hydrocodone, codeine, or tramadol. This is the combination the FDA's boxed warning is about.
- **Prescription sleep drugs** such as zolpidem (Ambien), and over-the-counter "PM" products.
- **Sedating antihistamines** such as diphenhydramine (Benadryl) or hydroxyzine. See why these are a poor pick after drinking in our page on [Benadryl for a hangover](/never-hungover/benadryl-for-hangover).
- **Gabapentin and pregabalin**, which add their own sedation and breathing effects. Our [gabapentin and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/gabapentin-and-alcohol) covers that combination.
- **Other sedating psychiatric medicines**, such as trazodone or some antipsychotics. See [trazodone and alcohol](/never-hungover/trazodone-and-alcohol).
- **Cannabis**, which adds its own impairment.

Even mild sleep supplements are worth thinking twice about on a night you've been drinking. Melatonin is far less sedating than clonazepam, but stacking sleep-promoting substances isn't wise. See [melatonin and alcohol](/never-hungover/melatonin-and-alcohol).

A note on pills that don't come from a pharmacy: counterfeit "Klonopin" or "Xanax" pills sold online or passed around socially can contain fentanyl or other potent drugs. Never take a pill that wasn't dispensed to you by a pharmacy.

## Don't Stop Klonopin Suddenly So You Can Drink

Some people decide to stop their clonazepam for a few days before a big event so they can drink. This is risky in a different way.

- **Clonazepam can cause physical dependence**, even when taken exactly as prescribed, especially after weeks or months of daily use.
- **Stopping suddenly can cause withdrawal.** Symptoms can include rebound anxiety and panic, insomnia, irritability, tremor, sweating, and in some cases seizures. In people who take clonazepam for epilepsy, stopping abruptly can trigger seizures directly.
- **Because the half-life is long, withdrawal can start days after the last dose**, which can catch people off guard right when they're drinking.
- **Alcohol withdrawal works through the same system.** Heavy, regular drinking followed by a sudden stop can also cause tremors, anxiety, and seizures, and having both in play makes things more complicated.

This is why the label tells prescribers to taper clonazepam gradually rather than stopping it all at once. If you want to stop or reduce Klonopin, do it with your prescriber's help. The same applies if you drink heavily most days and want to cut back: speak to a doctor first, because suddenly stopping heavy daily drinking can be medically risky in its own right.

For most social drinkers who take clonazepam, withdrawal isn't the issue. The issue is simply not overlapping the two.

## Emergency Signs: When to Call 911

An overdose involving clonazepam and alcohol can creep up quietly. The person may look like they're just deeply asleep.

**Call 911 right away if someone who has taken Klonopin (or an unknown pill) and alcohol:**

- Can't be woken up, or wakes only briefly and drifts off again
- Is breathing very slowly, shallowly, irregularly, or with long pauses, or is making loud snoring or gurgling sounds
- Has blue, gray, or pale lips or fingertips, or cold, clammy skin
- Has a very slow or weak pulse
- Is having a seizure
- Is vomiting while drowsy or confused

**While you wait for help:**

- Stay with them. Don't let them "sleep it off" alone.
- If they're breathing but not responsive, roll them onto their side so they don't choke if they vomit.
- If opioids or a counterfeit pill could be involved and you have naloxone (Narcan), give it. It won't reverse alcohol or clonazepam, but it can reverse a hidden opioid and won't harm them if there isn't one.
- Tell the responders exactly what was taken and roughly when, and bring the pill bottle if you can.

Hospitals have a medicine (flumazenil) that can reverse benzodiazepines, but it's used cautiously and only by medical teams because it can trigger seizures in some patients. There's no home remedy for this situation. Calling for help is the treatment.

If you're not sure whether something is an emergency, the US Poison Control line at **1-800-222-1222** is free, confidential, and open 24 hours.

## If You Take Klonopin and Have a Social Event Coming Up

You don't have to skip every social event because of your prescription. You do need to skip the alcohol.

- **Plan to go alcohol-free.** Many bars now carry decent alcohol-free beer, wine, and mocktails, and "I'm on medication" is a complete explanation that nobody questions.
- **Never adjust your dose on your own** to make room for drinking, in either direction.
- **Tell your prescriber if avoiding alcohol is hard.** It's a routine conversation, and it may change how they manage your treatment.
- **Tell a friend** you take clonazepam, so they know what an emergency looks like.

## Where DHM Fits (and Where It Doesn't)

We cover DHM (dihydromyricetin) a lot on this site, so it's worth being direct about it here.

**DHM does not make it safe to combine Klonopin and alcohol.** There's no good evidence that DHM or any other supplement reduces the sedation, memory loss, or breathing risk from this combination.

There's also a specific reason for caution. Animal and lab research suggests DHM works partly at the **GABA-A receptor**, the same place clonazepam acts. How DHM and benzodiazepines interact in people hasn't been studied. That doesn't prove a problem, but it's enough of a reason not to add it on your own. **If you take clonazepam, ask your prescriber or pharmacist before trying DHM.** Our [DHM medication interactions and safety guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025) goes into the overlap with other medicines.

No supplement is a substitute for not mixing alcohol with clonazepam. For the same topic with a shorter-acting benzodiazepine, see [Xanax and alcohol](/never-hungover/xanax-and-alcohol), and for the wider group of sedating medicines, see [Ativan and alcohol](/never-hungover/ativan-and-alcohol).

## The Bottom Line

- Klonopin (clonazepam) and alcohol both slow the brain through the GABA-A system, and together they cause more sedation, more memory loss, and slower breathing than either alone.
- Clonazepam's half-life of roughly 30 to 40 hours means it's still active the next day, and daily users always have it in their system. Skipping a dose doesn't create a safe window.
- There's no amount of alcohol known to be safe with clonazepam. Don't drink while you're taking it.
- Don't use Klonopin for hangover anxiety or to sleep after drinking, and don't stop it suddenly to make room for drinking.
- If someone who took Klonopin and drank can't be woken or is breathing slowly, call 911 and stay with them.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can you drink alcohol while taking Klonopin?**

You shouldn't. Klonopin (clonazepam) and alcohol both slow the brain through the GABA-A system, and together they can cause heavy sedation, blackouts, falls, and dangerously slow breathing. The prescribing information tells patients to avoid alcohol, and there's no amount known to be safe. If you have questions about drinking on your prescription, ask your prescriber or pharmacist.

**How long after taking Klonopin can I drink alcohol?**

There's no official waiting period that applies to everyone. Clonazepam's half-life is about 30 to 40 hours, so a single dose stays active for more than a day and takes several days to clear almost completely. If you take it daily, it never fully clears while you're on it. Ask your prescriber or pharmacist what's sensible for your dose instead of guessing.

**Is clonazepam and alcohol the same as Klonopin and alcohol?**

Yes. Clonazepam is the generic name and Klonopin is the brand name for the same drug. Generic clonazepam tablets and orally disintegrating tablets carry the same warnings about alcohol as the brand.

**Is one drink okay on Klonopin?**

No. There's no amount of alcohol known to be safe with clonazepam, and the label doesn't list one. Because clonazepam stays active for more than a day, the safe approach is no alcohol at all while you're taking it. If someone has mixed the two and is hard to wake or breathing slowly, call 911.

**Can I take Klonopin for a hangover or to sleep after drinking?**

It's a bad idea. Alcohol can still be in your blood the next morning, and at bedtime after drinking it almost certainly is, so you'd be combining the two. Using a sedative to calm the rebound anxiety from alcohol can also build a risky pattern. In people who drink heavily every day, morning shakiness and anxiety can be early alcohol withdrawal, which needs a doctor rather than self-treatment.

**What are the signs of a Klonopin and alcohol overdose?**

Call 911 if someone can't be woken, is breathing very slowly, shallowly, or with long pauses, has blue or gray lips or fingertips, has a very slow pulse, is having a seizure, or is vomiting while drowsy or confused. Stay with them, roll them onto their side if they're breathing but unresponsive, and give naloxone if opioids or a counterfeit pill could be involved.

**Is Klonopin more dangerous with alcohol than Xanax?**

Both carry the same core risk because they act on the same GABA-A receptor. The main difference is timing. Clonazepam lasts much longer, with a half-life of roughly 30 to 40 hours compared with around 11 hours for immediate-release alprazolam, so its overlap with alcohol can stretch into the next day or beyond. How dangerous a given combination is depends mostly on the doses and amount of alcohol involved.

**Should I skip my Klonopin dose so I can drink?**

No. Skipping doses doesn't clear clonazepam from your system because of its long half-life, and stopping suddenly after regular use can cause withdrawal symptoms, including seizures in some people. Never change your dose on your own. Ask your prescriber how to handle alcohol and events ahead of time.

**Can I take DHM if I'm on Klonopin?**

Check with your prescriber or pharmacist first. In animal studies DHM appears to act partly at GABA-A receptors, the same system clonazepam works on, and its interaction with benzodiazepines in people hasn't been studied. There is also no good evidence that DHM or any supplement makes it safe to combine Klonopin and alcohol.
